content: The two police officers killed in a crash with five suspected joyriders on Saturday morning have been pictured on several front pages on Monday morning, including the Times. The paper includes tributes from the families of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, under the headline: "Family's pain beyond words over police deaths". Alongside the two police officers, the Metro also pictures the five "youngsters" who died in the high-speed Middlesbrough crash, whom it names as Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Jacob Matusiak, 23, and Makai Saddington, 18. University graduates are facing the worst job market on record, the Telegraph says, suggesting vacancies have fallen 45% from this time last year. It notes that it comes as a record number of teenagers head to university next month, adding that the latest numbers represent a "steep challenge" for new Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The Guardian says that Monday will see Burnham announce that the UK will help Ukraine make its own long-range missiles. The prime minister will arrive in Ukraine later today to mark its independence day, the paper reports, where he will say that the European defence company MBDA will be allowed to declassify information about the UK-made components of Storm Shadow missiles. The Guardian adds that, while the announcement will likely take years to have an impact on the war, it could escalate tensions with Moscow at a "fraught" time in UK-Russian relations. Universities are also the lead for the i Paper, which says the prime minister is prepared to reduce the "hefty" tuition fees for Europeans studying in the UK in exchange for "substantial concessions on trade". The paper says Brussels has long demanded lower rates as part of a youth mobility deal for under-30s visas, but the UK has so far resisted due to warnings from universities that it could "blow a hole" in their finances. The Financial Times has focused on an upcoming speech from US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh, where he is expected to attempt to "soothe investors' nerves" as signs of economic strain mount. The paper suggests that the speech, which will be made on Friday at the annual Jackson Hole symposium, could be a crunch moment for one of Donald Trump's key economic appointees. A warning from the National Crime Agency (NCA) is the main story for the Daily Mail, which declares "Children are 'not safe' on the internet". The head of the agency, Graeme Biggar, has told the paper that every day sees an average of 400 cases of suspected child sexual exploitation flagged to the NCA. Catherine, Princess of Wales, beams on the front page of the Sun, which reads: "We're all grin it together". The paper says the Royal family are presenting a "united front" ahead of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's return to the UK later this month. "Let's talk about assisted dying, Mr Burnham... while I still can" reads the Daily Express, after interviewing terminally ill father Phil Newby. The campaigner, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease 12 years ago, has asked Burnham for a meeting to discuss the legislation before he is no longer able. The front page of the Daily Mirror is dedicated to its own campaign on water safety, Save Lives for Sam, after a number of drownings over the summer. The paper says at least 56 people this year have drowned in the UK, with their families signing an open letter to the prime minister pleading with him to meet them and "prevent more lives from being lost". The Hong Kong placement is the largest primary follow-on by a locally listed company, and it is roughly half of what the EU has committed to its entire AI gigafactory programme Alibaba Group provisional office at Xiong’an Alibaba is placing HK$80bn, about $10.2bn, of new shares in Hong Kong and says all net proceeds will go to AI infrastructure and capabilities. It comes days after the company reported a 75% fall in quarterly net profit driven by that same spending. Alibaba is going to the market for money to spend on AI, and it is not being coy about the proportion. The company is placing HK$80bn of new shares in Hong Kong, around $10.2bn, and says 100% of net proceeds will fund its full stack AI capabilities including infrastructure. The size is a record on two counts. Alibaba calls it the largest primary follow-on offering ever by a Hong Kong-listed company, and the biggest Regulation S equity offering on record, meaning shares sold to investors outside the United States. Globally it lands third this year. Only Alphabet, which raised $85bn in equity, and Intel have run larger primary follow-ons in 2026. The timing is what makes it interesting. Three days earlier Alibaba reported that quarterly net profit had fallen 75%, with capital expenditure up 75% to 67.68bn yuan in the April to June quarter. The spending is buying growth somewhere. Cloud and AI revenue rose 45% to 48.44bn yuan, and the company says its AI model services now run above 16bn yuan in annual recurring revenue. Chief executive Eddie Wu has been direct about the sequence. “In order to be able to capture that future growth, we first need to make these capex investments to build out the necessary compute capacity,” he said. This tops up a commitment already half spent. Alibaba pledged 380bn yuan over three years in early 2025, reports suggest it is considering raising that to 480bn yuan, and Wu says its own chips could lift margins substantially as they scale. Set that against Europe’s headline number. The EU has committed around €20bn to its AI gigafactory programme, so a single afternoon’s placement in Hong Kong is roughly half the continent’s flagship compute budget. Alibaba is not a distant competitor in this. It opened two availability zones in Paris in June, its third European hub after Germany and Britain, positioning itself as a sovereign option for European customers. Brussels is building rules that point the other way. The Cloud and AI Development Act proposed in June sets a four-tier sovereignty framework whose stricter levels require EU ownership and operational independence, which a Chinese-headquartered provider cannot easily satisfy. So the two trends run straight at each other. Europe wants more compute and is writing rules about whose it can be, while the company raising the money is expanding here regardless. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Ever thought that car speakers sound better than almost any other speakers? Well, it's not always the speaker. Car interiors are controlled environments, where speakers have predictable performance and naturally good sound insulation due to fabric ceilings, foam seating, and smooth angles for sound waves to bounce off. Stock car speakers can be an afterthought, which is why there's a big car audio market. People also think of upgrading speakers over the stock head unit, which is a cheap way to upgrade audio quality in older cars. Unless buyers are getting a sports model that specifically states it has a branded sound system, people are usually stuck with basic door speakers. No amp, headunit, or subwoofer is usually included, but there are plenty of aftermarket options — from a budget upgrade to serious sonic power. An expensive setup doesn't always mean a good one, and looking at what's included in bundles and real-world performance can often result in drivers saving a small fortune on the specs they need instead of financially flexing. We've picked out five different car speaker options with superb audio quality relative to their price point. There's a car speaker upgrade for every kind of listener that offers a great upgrade over stock cones for every kind of budget, from a $399.95 2-speaker upgrade with glass-fiber woofer cones and 300-watt peak power to premium and tuned $1,370.99 speaker kits that sound like nothing else on the market. Let's get into it: The Focal Mobile ES 165 KX2E is a premium beast of a car sound system. It's a best seller because it offers the best dollar-to-performance value for a 2-way 6.5-inch component kit. It's not cheap, currently $1,370.99 at Amazon, but there are plenty of good reasons why it's worth every penny. For starters, it features a signature K2 sandwich cone made up of a foam core between aramid fiber and fiberglass. Its FRAK aluminum "M-profile" inverted dome tweeter puts out detailed yet smooth highs, meaning this financial investment doesn't sound like it's coming through a Pringles tin. They're built in France and are thoughtfully designed instead of being generic mass-produced cones, which is illustrated in its rigid aluminum basket and TMD surround to reduce distortion. There's nothing wrong with metal and rock music, but added distortion from generic low-quality speakers that can't handle some frequencies and higher volumes isn't cool.  They're incredibly efficient by just drawing 2 ohms from its amp, meaning it can put out louder volumes with less power draw vs. the industry standard 4 ohms. Frequency response is also solid at 55Hz low-end to a 32kHz high-end, with 20kHz being the limit of what humans can actually hear. Overall, this is a great choice. Alpine R2-S65C is a solid mid-range choice with Carbon-fiber-reinforced woofers for clear sound while holding up impressive midbass for the price. Its frequency response is solid, from a 65Hz low-end to a 40kHz high end, handling high-resolution audio with no issues. In fact, it's Hi-Res audio certified and delivered by its magnesium hard-dome tweeters and fast transient response. Alpine is a reliable name with plenty of options across all budgets, but this one hits that sweet spot for a mid-range kit with 100W RMS power handling. There are some good specifications and features with the R2-S65C to warrant its $399.99 price tag. It has a ferrite magnet structure, specifically ceramic magnets, with reliable thermal stability perfect for controlling woofer cones. HAMR surround (high-amplitude multi-roll), which is a rubber surround for the woofer cone to efficiently move air while staying cool. It produces enhanced low-frequency control, resulting in tight and clean bass.  Two premium-grade in-line crossover networks that split audio signals clearly before reaching the speaker, resulting in damage prevention, less distortion, and improved overall sound clarity. For drivers who want a decent upgrade with some nice features without going over the $500 mark, Alpine R2-S65C is solid value for replacing two stock 6.5-inch car speakers. A solid budget choice for two 6.5-inch component speakers is the JL Audio C2-650 sitting at $329.99 right now. Featuring mineral-filled polypropylene cones that are a good fit in most cars, it comes with multiple mounting patterns on the woofer frame itself for an easy fit providing drivers are replacing stock 6.5-inch speakers. Power handling is pretty standard at 120 watts per set, or 60 watts per speaker, with 91dB of sensitivity with Butyl rubber speaker surrounds to calm any distortion, with a surprising amount of bass depth for the woofer cone size. The tweeters feature 0.75-inch silk dome diaphragms that put out smooth yet-solid highs and less fatigue on and off axis, coming complete with three levels of attenuation and a tweeter protector. There's an argument to be made on silk vs. metal tweeters, but for the price point, those looking for a warm tone will be very happy with C2-650 component kit. Other tech nerdy specifications include a 1-inch voice coil on Kapton former, premium Mylar capacitors, premium air-core inductors, a flat symmetrical roll spider, and included protective speaker grilles. For under $350 with a 1-year manufacturer's warranty, JL Audio C2-650 is a great choice for a budget component kit. First-time drivers rocking a cheap car to keep insurance premiums down will likely benefit from upgrading their car speaker system to the Kicker 46CSS654. It's a component system for a very reasonable price point at $152.96, especially considering the 6.5-inch speakers feature Polypropylene woofers and titanium dome tweeters. This delivers ultra-clean bass thanks to the extended voice coil and higher volumes in high frequencies, which is helped along by Neodymium tweeter magnets and phase plugs that help with distortion and better clarity. This component system isn't going to compete with one double its price, but it's good value for money. It has 100W power handling and a 35Hz low-end to 21kHz high-end, which is going to be an instant upgrade on a budget car. It's proper component sound at a price point that borders impulse buy territory, and if I was still driving my Nissan Micra from 2012, it would be a decent upgrade. It uses UV-treated poly-foam surrounds to help with direct heat or direct sunlight, with three tweeter mounting options for flush, angled, and surface levels. Kicker 46CSS654 is designed to be a worthwhile step up from dull factory speakers, so for someone who wants to pack a better punch while listening to Metallica but doesn't expect it to sound like an arena show. Looking for an easy car speaker upgrade for under $100? The Polk Audio DB652 is a 6.5-inch 2-way coaxial speaker that's a far simpler install than component kits, with a 40Hz low end, a 22kHz frequency response, and a 300W peak. It features a Polypropylene woofer cone and a 3/4-inch silk dome tweeter designed to deliver smooth highs while being very durable.  It's IP56 marine-rated too, which is a great feature to have on a car speaker that's going to be installed in an active user's car. It bats away heat, handles moisture, and is UV light-treated, making it a solid choice for an off-road car or convertible too. It's not going to go up against $500 and higher speakers, but it's an honest buy at $85 on Amazon, with some nice additional proprietary features from Polk Audio such as Dynamic Balance. Laser imaging tech has been used during the design process to identify the best speaker materials to combine, resulting in low to no distortion. Drivers will likely want to buy at least two Polk Audio DB652 to replace the front passenger and driver-side door stock speakers. Even with a minimum $170 price tag that includes mounting hardware for 6.5-inch car speakers and grilles, it's a cheap and easy upgrade with noticeable results in budget and older model cars. There are also some free and easy ways to improve all car audio systems, such as using on-board EQ or optimizing balance and fade. We decided to go with superior-quality car speakers based on budget, because anyone can make a list of expensive component systems that only a certain percentage of people can afford and justify. So by cross-referencing expert roundups with best-seller details from online retailers and average customer reviews, we put together an article with a car speaker for pretty much everyone.  Specifications prioritized here include sensitivity, RMS power handling, frequency response, and build material, which we feel are the most important factors when shopping for a quality car speaker upgrade. Some people want a plug-and-play upgrade, which is why it was important to include drop-in coaxial speakers for a quick boost in audio quality, alongside component bundles for enthusiast buyers. Focusing on what makes the woofer cone and tweeter special, such as unique cone structures and materials or silk and metal tweeters, was also a big factor in finding car speakers that stand out in an oversaturated market. There are picks here that draw power from the factory head unit alongside component units that feature their own head or amp to handle high-resolution audio. Best sellers have also been taken into consideration, but they don't always represent the full picture. We've also looked at spec sheets for each speaker choice to make sure every recommendation is worth its price tag. Found this useful? It might be possible to outrun your next rent payment — if you live with roommates. Nike is offering a unique — and highly relevant — prize to two winners of a street race in New York City on August 29: "1 month of free rent." "Step to the starting line on Orchard Street for a chance to win one month of rent paid," the company says. Participants, who will be chosen by a random drawing, will race in a series of 100-meter dashes, advancing through an undisclosed number of heats before racing in a final round. At the end of it all, the two fastest participants will each earn up to $4,000, which Nike is marketing as enough for a month's rent. For many New Yorkers, though, that might not cover it. The median Manhattan rental price for a market-rate apartment, where the race is set to occur, soared to $5,000 last month, according to an August report from The Real Deal and appraisal firm Samuel Miller. Should the winners of the races hail from Queens or Brooklyn, the $4,000 prize will likely be enough, but not by much. According to data from Apartments.com, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Queens is $3,605. In Brooklyn, it's $3,082. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made lowering the city's astronomical housing costs a centerpiece of his administration. His signature rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments takes effect this fall, while City Hall is pursuing a broader plan to build and preserve 200,000 affordable homes over the next decade. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. Representatives for Mamdani did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday. The race comes as Nike tries to recapture some of the cultural cachet it's lost in recent years. CEO Elliott Hill, a Nike veteran who returned to lead the company in 2024, has been working to refocus the brand on sports, rebuild relationships with retailers, and revive product innovation after years of losing ground to competitors like Hoka and On. The turnaround has shown signs of progress in North America, but it's been slow going. Nike's shares remain well below their 2021 peak, while weakness in China and other challenges continue to weigh on the company. No comments right now, check back later. Samsung, Google, and Apple might be the biggest players in the North American market, but Motorola does pretty well for itself. In fact, Motorola has consistently had a larger market share than Google in the U.S. over the last five quarters. And yet, when you head to a store or open an online shopping platform, Google Pixel cases, screen protectors, and accessories are much easier to find than Motorola accessories. Mainstream brands like Spigen, OtterBox, and CASETiFY happily cater to Pixel phones, including the more niche ones like the Pixel 10 Pro Fold. But when it comes to Motorola flagships and foldables like the Razr Fold and Razr Ultra 2026, most of these name brands are MIA. It's a real head-scratcher.      I can't fault an accessory maker for skipping a phone brand because of profitability concerns. Companies exist to make money, and when they fear losses due to demand concerns, it's sensible to remain pragmatic. What I can't make sense of is the apparent lack of confidence that these phone case and accessory brands seem to have in Motorola. Why are these companies still not catering to them, especially now that Motorola holds about 50% of the foldable smartphone market in the U.S.? I reached out to dozens of the top, most popular case makers who regularly offer products for Samsung, Google, and Apple to get some answers. My question was simple: Why aren't name-brand case makers prioritizing Motorola's flagships and foldables? Almost all of them replied, but Android Central has kept some of their names anonymous to protect the source's identity. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android      OtterBox was one of the few brands that went on the record, citing demand as the key reason. They weren't alone; at least five to six others echoed the same sentiment, including one of the most respectable case makers in the business. "We evaluate our device case portfolio based on customer demand and overall device adoption. While OtterBox has supported Motorola devices in the past, our current focus is on delivering protection for the devices used most widely by our customers." An up-and-coming high-end case maker also doubled down on demand holding them back, but mentioned that they might open up support for Motorola devices in the future: "From a case maker's perspective, product coverage decisions are primarily driven by device demand, market scale, and the broader ecosystem adoption rather than any individual brand preference. For major launches, we typically prioritize devices that demonstrate the largest global user base and strongest accessory demand at scale, which currently tends to concentrate around a small number of flagship smartphone lines. Motorola’s recent foldables and flagships have certainly generated interest within the industry, particularly around design and form factor innovation. However, compared to the leading platforms, the overall installed base and accessory demand for these devices is still relatively limited at this stage." The brand went on to say that they might consider expanding their accessory range to support Motorola once there is "clear and sustained traction for specific models or form factors."      Another affordable accessory brand that focuses more on chargers said it mainly comes down to resource prioritization. This brand offers cases and screen protectors, but charging tech for Apple and Samsung is their primary concern. They stated that launching an entirely new phone case lineup "would require additional investment, such as product design, manufacturing, and human resources. Our company may not be able to fully support this at the present stage." TORRAS, a brand that focuses on magnetic phone cases as much as it does on chargers and power banks, shared that focusing on a single foldable makes it easier to perfect their craft. "TORRAS’ focus in the foldable category has been on building long-term engineering experience within the Samsung Fold ecosystem over multiple generations. Each generation brings different mechanical and structural challenges, which helps us continuously refine key areas such as hinge protection, ultra-thin structures, magnetic alignment, and overall durability performance. By staying consistent within a single foldable architecture, TORRAS is able to deepen our R&D in a more systematic and iterative way, improving product reliability through continuous optimization over time."      One brand saw this lack of support as an opportunity and took a personal request from Android Central's Nicholas Sutrich to heart. Texas-born case maker Thinborne had initially scrapped its plans to launch a Moto Razr Fold case, just weeks after announcing it. I was very disappointed, because there are very few premium-grade cases that match the thinness and lightness of something from Thinborne. Sutrich reached out to Thinborne after hearing the news, concerned about the lack of decent cases for Motorola foldables. Thinborne admits that their entire $32,000 investment in making this happen could very well result in a loss. "After hesitating twice, we decided to make it happen — not for profits, but to make sure there is still an option for people looking for a premium minimalist case for their Motorola Razr Fold." It is truly admirable that while bigger name brands shied away from the task, a small company like Thinborne stepped up. It created perhaps the best Motorola Razr Fold case we could ask for: a thin, lightweight aramid fiber case with MagSafe support, so you can take advantage of MagSafe accessories. Plus, it comes in different colors like Crimson and Navy, so you can give your Razr Fold a bit of life.      Dbrand shed more light on this topic, noting that, beyond demand, Motorola's lack of support for third-party retailers is another limiting factor. "Motorola doesn't engage 3rd party consumer accessory manufacturers the way other OEMs do. Google has Made for Google. Microsoft has Designed for Xbox. Samsung has SMAPP. These structured programs give established brands the lead time to be ready at launch (not to mention, B2B opportunities that amplify attach to the hardware TAM). With Motorola, our starting gun for development is when consumer hardware hits shelves. By that point, we're already too late." The brand went on to acknowledge that scale and numbers aren't everything. Far smaller, more niche brands like Minimal have approached Dbrand to make accessories for their devices happen. It's the effort that the smartphone maker put into collaborating with Dbrand that materialized into Dbrand skins for Minimal phones. "Motorola's lack of engagement with the 3rd party ecosystem makes it structurally challenging to show up at the 'peak of interest' launch moment that matters." Motorola could easily do the same, but seemingly chooses not to.      I went to Motorola to hear it straight from the horse's mouth and asked whether they were aware of how accessory brands felt about Motorola's devices, and whether they were planning to address these concerns about demand and collaborative efforts. Motorola's response was very vague. They don't seem to recognize that they have an accessory problem. In fact, Motorola emphasized that they "actively [develop] a robust partnership program to expand the range of high-quality accessory options for [their] customers". The rest of the response felt like standard boilerplate and did not even seem to address the concerns from top accessory brands: "Today, we proudly collaborate with a number of partners to anchor our official licensed cases and accessories initiative. Through this established program, we co-develop and validate products with trusted third-party accessory makers. This collaborative approach ensures that every product adheres to Motorola’s strict standards for quality, safety, and seamless customer experience. We are continuously expanding this ecosystem and welcome deeper strategic partnerships with leading accessory brands to deliver the premium experience our customers expect." At the end of the day, I learned that most brands still perceive Motorola as having low demand, even when the numbers suggest otherwise. Meanwhile, Motorola is wearing rose-colored glasses or has seemingly convinced itself that it is doing a fine job of it and that there is no accessory support problem. This can be fixed, however. Perhaps if Motorola were to extend an olive branch, it might move things along. If they want third-party accessory support to improve, they will have to put in the effort and make it easier for accessory and case makers to cater to their devices. Based on everything I have heard, I hope Motorola will follow through. It could also improve smartphone sales, as accessory support is a major concern for consumers when buying phones. Perhaps if official "Made for Moto" accessories were to appear in the wild, a lot more people would be interested in buying Motorola phones, especially if they came from top-tier brands like Dbrand, Spigen, and CASETiFY. Recently, Mophie debuted four new power banks for the iPhone. They slide nicely into your pocket, come in two finishes, offer built-in cables, and pack 5000mAh or 10000mAh of capacity. They’re by no means the smallest battery banks on the market, though they hit a price point that makes them worthwhile. Mophie’s new PowerStation Plus battery banks come in Standard and Signature variants, each with 5000mAh and 10000mAh capacity options. Both the standard and signature versions come in the same footprints, though the signature version comes with a nicer finish and comes with braided cables. All four versions include integrated USB-C cables for charging your device in a pinch, though they aren’t retractable. The cable is integrated on the side of the bank, and you can slide it out of place when you need to charge. The lower three variants of the PowerStation Plus come with one built-in cable, whereas the Signature 10K version has two braided cables. With the additional USB-C port, this allows you to charge up to three devices at once. Phillip Grant is feeling optimistic. He thinks he's the best man to operate Mayor Zohran Mamdani's city-run supermarkets. Along with being a former city economic development executive and construction entrepreneur, he's a New Yorker who's shocked that an orange costs $2 at his local gas station. We're walking the perimeter of a vacant city-owned lot in East Harlem. It's the future spot for La Marqueta, one of five planned stores set to open by the end of Mamdani's first term — all of which will offer a 30% discount on core goods like fruit, vegetables, and dairy. It's also the most expensive location, accounting for $30 million of the $70 million the mayor has set aside to launch the initiative. The administration is looking for established grocers who know the food business and can take on day-to-day store management. If he were to be named operator, Grant said he "would be looking for a really strategic partner" in the city, "that could knock on those doors that we can't get to and have an ear to the street." Engaging with the public will be key. Over the past few weeks, I've had dozens of conversations about Mamdani's city-run stores — one of his buzziest promises aimed at lowering the cost of living in one of the most expensive cities in the world. Some New Yorkers welcome a solution for high food prices, while others are concerned nearby mom-and-pop shops will lose customers in an already profit-poor industry. A few hopeful operators, like Grant, said they know the highs and lows of the grocery industry and want to be part of Mamdani's solution. The East Harlem lot is flanked by a slew of small shops: Meat markets, produce stands, grocers, and convenience stores. It's a block-and-a-half north of the existing La Marqueta municipal market, a city-owned building where local vendors sell everything from embroidered clothing to pastries and benefit from government-subsidized rent. Yesi Morillo has run a gift shop and bookstore in that municipal market for nearly two years. "It's been a struggle," she told me, and she rarely turns a profit. Morillo hopes that traffic from the city-run store will boost her customer base, but she feels that she and other vendors have received very little communication from government leaders about how their businesses will be affected. Existing vendors in the area "have been neglected," she said. It's frustrating to think that, "'Oh, you're going to spend all this money on building this new infrastructure and the basic things that we have been asking for don't get done,'" Morillo said, adding, "If I had an opportunity to sit with Mamdani, I would say do not do a supermarket that's going to be lower cost for people. There are supermarkets here that have been here for decades that have been serving the community and where the community feels comfortable shopping." Economic Development Corporation leaders told me that vendors like Morillo will not be moved into the new grocery store space, and the municipal market and public grocery store will remain two separate entities. The surrounding neighborhood is densely built and near major transit lines, with an average weekly foot traffic of 4,300 people. The EDC said it chose East Harlem for the Manhattan location for a combination of reasons, like existing city-owned property, transit access, local income levels, and population density, but did not share criteria specifics. The second location for the stores — opening early next year — will be at La Peninsula, a building in the Bronx. The other three will be in Queens, Brooklyn, and Staten Island. In late July, the EDC — the quasi-public arm of NYC's government that manages city-owned property — started taking applications from potential operators for the stores. The EDC will offer them rent-free store space, while the city will set branding and pricing standards. Qiana Mickie, executive director of the Mayor's Office of Urban Agriculture, told me her team will also work with the stores to shorten supply chains and lean on locally grown produce, which she hopes will help lower food prices. Some private grocers are skeptical. Mark Jaffe, a founder of the Multicultural Business Coalition, which represents local grocery chains, bodegas, and other vendors, worries about how this will impact his network. "The policy of feeding the hungry is good, the cost of living in New York is high. Low-wage earners could use some help," he said. "Our argument, and we've spoken to many people in the legal field, is that this is not a well-planned way to feed people." It's a sentiment I've heard from several small business groups and industry analysts. Food is a tough business: Profit margins for grocery stores are typically between 1% and 3%. Some vendors say they won't be able to compete with a big store that can offer customers a discount on the city's dime. "One lucky person will get the winning bid to run all five of these grocery stores," Jaffee said. "It's gotta be a pretty nice position." So far, operator applicants have a lot of questions. Based on public filings, the group is asking city leaders how the Mamdani administration will deliver the 30% discount — and whether they will need to shoulder the cost of lowering food prices for customers, especially if inflation worsens. Other queries focus on how much operators are expected to pay their staff, and if EDC plans to reimburse operators for spoiled food or costly supply hiccups. For many of these, the answer is along the lines of "it depends." The EDC said it's still reviewing which specific food subsidies it will offer operators beyond free rent, and whether it will also offer support to nearby private grocers. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. "I think it's a cool concept because everybody needs a break at the cash register," another applicant on the tour, who said they've spent their career in grocery fulfillment and brick-and-mortar stores, told me. Roughly a fifth of New Yorkers are food insecure, and the cost of food in US cities has jumped by 25% in the past five years. Both supporters and skeptics of the NYC -run stores agreed on this cost-of-living problem. Critics of the city-run supermarkets say that they will be too expensive to run in the long term, or wish the city were directly supporting social safety net programs or small businesses instead of opening its own stores. Valerie Imbruce, who researches community food systems at Washington University and wrote the NYC groceries-focused book "From Farm to Canal Street," told me that the $70 million allocated to the initiative is "going to essentially build grocery stores and have a branding campaign. That's the part that I'm skeptical about because I know how far that money can go for more localized initiatives that could have a larger cumulative effect." Grant knows that Mamdani's stores will need to find a way to sustain themselves. He wants to help. Now, it's a waiting game until the city chooses an operator. Especially since some third-party retailers still have the OnePlus 15R and OnePlus 15 in stock. But if you are to get your hands on one now, how many updates will the phone get, and if you own an older model, will it make it to Android 18? The latest OnePlus phones are currently on OxygenOS 16, which is based on Android 16. OnePlus released OxygenOS 16 in North America in December 2025, about seven months after Google released the final stable version of Android 16. Android 18 is expected to release in mid-2027; OPPO and OnePlus will likely have the next major Android update rolled out a few months after, based on the update history. OnePlus phones with multiple years of support since 2024 should be eligible for Android 18. Regarding whether it's worth keeping or buying a OnePlus phone in 2026, OnePlus said current users in Europe and North America will receive after-sales support, and all software updates and warranties will be honored, meaning the process stays the same as any other manufacturer still servicing phones in the region. However, if you're in the market for a second-hand OnePlus device, note that the company also doesn't offer long-term software support like Samsung and Google do. Still, OnePlus phones usually get four major Android updates and about five or six years of security patches; that's for both flagship and midrange devices. At the same time, budget Nord N models get only about a year of updates and two to three years of security patches. That means OnePlus models released in 2024 or later are eligible for Android 18, assuming no delays with the release schedule: You can also expect the OnePlus 16 series, OnePlus Nord 7, and possibly the OnePlus 17 to support Android 18, but these phones won't be available in the U.S. OnePlus phones have OxygenOS installed, which is still separate from ColorOS in the U.S. However, that will no longer be the case, as ColorOS will be the unified custom Android skin on OnePlus phones going forward — technically, they already share the same codebase. The transition to the new, more bloat-heavy or feature-rich OS should happen when Android 17 releases. North American OnePlus phones that should receive ColorOS 17 (based on the Android 17 update) should also be expected to update to ColorOS 18. This upgrade is optional, but after OxygenOS 16, the software will no longer be available. Normally, when a major stock Android update is released, manufacturers take time to release it with their custom skin update, usually to ensure compatibility with the software layer. The bad news for European and North American users is that they won't be able to join the beta program directly without changing their region through a non-local SIM card. Normally, OnePlus has always had an open and closed beta test program you could apply for through the About phone settings, but availability depended on region. Now, with the official market exit, users won't be able to test features before they're released.

The legal software company has launched Tenet, its first proprietary model, after years of routing customer work through models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The base it chose is the detail worth stopping on. Tenet is post-trained on Kimi K3, the open-weight model released in July by the Chinese startup Moonshot, in work Harvey says it did with Fireworks AI. Consider who is on the cap table. OpenAI is an investor in Harvey alongside Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz, so a company valued at $15.5bn has built its flagship on a Chinese base to reduce its dependence on its own backer. The commercial logic is unsubtle. Every model call Harvey makes on a customer’s behalf is an invoice from a rival, and owning the engine turns a variable cost into a fixed one. Quality is the other argument. Cofounder Gabe Pereyra, formerly of Google DeepMind, says Harvey already routes tasks to whichever model suits them, and Tenet adds an option shaped around legal work specifically. The training material was manufactured. Harvey hired lawyers, on staff and through firms including Mercor and Snorkel, to invent mock disputes and case files and then grade how well models reasoned through them. Europe’s answer to Harvey is Swedish. Legora is chasing a $10bn valuation and selling to many of the same firms, which makes the choice of base model a competitive question as much as a technical one. For a European buyer the AI Act is the next question. A company that modifies someone else’s general purpose model becomes the provider of the modified version only when the change is significant, with the Commission’s guidelines using roughly a third of the original training compute as the indicative marker. A post-train almost certainly falls well below that. President Donald Trump made more than 1,000 stock trades in June, according to an ethics filing published on Saturday—including buying stock in SpaceX over a week after its IPO and trading major tech and defense stocks doing business with the U.S. government, including Palantir. The stock trades were published by the Office of Government Ethics, listing over 1,000 individual sales and purchases of shares in June—although the form does not provide an exact value of each transaction, instead listing a range. Trump’s largest single transaction was the June 22 sale of shares of a Vanguard exchange traded fund, offloading between $5 million and $25 million of the ETF. The other major trades were in major American financial services stocks, including a purchase between $1 million and $5 million of Berkshire Hathaway, and similarly valued purchases of Visa, Mastercard and Cintas. Trump bought and sold shares of the same company multiple times—for example, he sold shares of Palantir twice, including a sale worth up to $1 million on June 18, but he also bought shares of the company for smaller amounts three times, including a purchase valued between $100,001 and $250,000 on June 24. Trump’s accounts also purchased and sold stock in major American tech companies like Meta, Broadcom, Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia. He also notably bought SpaceX stock worth between $15,001 and $50,000 on June 23, about 11 days after its initial public offering, as the company is poised to make billions of dollars through government contracts for satellites, the Wall Street Journal reported. The White House has previously insisted Trump’s finances were placed in a blind trust after he took office. However, it is still unclear exactly who is controlling these stock transactions. In May, Eric Trump, the president’s son and executive vice president of the Trump Organization, said the president’s accounts are “managed by independent third-party financial institutions,” and “neither President Trump, his family, nor The Trump Organization has any role in selecting, directing, approving, influencing or soliciting specific investments.” However, Democrats have still called this arrangement into question, as well as the “unprecedented” volume of trading that has gone on during his second term in office. In a letter signed by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the lawmakers estimate he made 14,000 stock trades in 2025 worth up to $1.06 billion, for an average of about 50 trades per day. Forbes has reached out to the White House for further comment about the most recent trades. In a statement provided to Bloomberg and other outlets, the White House said Trump’s stock trades are made using “computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000.” $2.4 billion. Notably, this figure does not include his stock trades, which were mostly reinvested in the market. Most of this newfound success instead came from his cryptocurrency ventures. "For a UK fish they are the most exciting and spectacular you can get by a country mile, no question." Catching an Atlantic bluefin tuna is often a career highlight for an angler. Last weekend a commercial vessel's crew caught and landed a 338kg fish off the coast of Whitby, becoming the first to do so in the North Sea for an estimated 60 years.  The following day, they did it again, with the story generating national and international headlines. After decades away, the species - dubbed the "Rolls Royce of the sea" - is thought to have returned to the Yorkshire coast in recent years. There are hopes its re-emergence could lead to a renaissance for "tunny" fishing, as it is still known in Scarborough and Whitby. In the 1930s the rich and famous flocked to Scarborough for the chance to catch the prized tunny for sport. The bluefin tuna, a migratory species, originally arrived in North Sea waters in search of herring to feed on when stocks of the latter were healthy. Their presence was soon spotted by local fishermen and "word spread", according to Mark Vesey, chair of the Scarborough Maritime Heritage Centre. "It became big game hunting for some very wealthy gentlemen," says Vesey. "All these people were well-to-do. Some of them went off hunting fish in the Bahamas or big game in Africa. That was their sport, their hobby. "It was really about catching it as a sport and having it weighed and being pictured standing next to it." The catches were incredible and many were recorded by the Scarborough Tunny Club. In 1933 Lorenzo Mitchell-Henry, an Irish angler, caught an 386kg (851lb) tunny off the coast of Whitby, which remains a British record for the biggest landed. "These things are just solid, pure muscle," explains Rupert Drury, who has been fishing for more than half a century. Drury, 60, caught a tunny off the coast of Whitby in 2024, describing the feat as "the pinnacle of my fishing career and all-time best catches". "You need the adequate strength of gear and adequate strength of character and stamina to be able to pull them in, they are heavyweight things," says the 60-year-old Drury recalls needing an hour-and-a-half, as well as the support of his crewmate Andy Watson, the pull the fish in. "The challenge is you are fishing for something that's hard to find, hard to hook, and is incredibly strong," he says. "It's a physical thing as much as anything, that's why it's called sport fishing." Unsurprisingly, the anglers who visited Scarborough were proud of their catches and keen to show off their achievements. The British Tunny Club was established there in 1933 and would play host to members of high society after a day spent fishing. "The would all meet there and smoke their pipes and display their photos with these great big tunny fish," says Vesey. "Often the only thing they kept was the tail fin, they would have that stuffed and kept on the wall. "As far as we know the fish didn't get eaten, sometimes they would give them to farmers to use as fertiliser. The strong flavour of the tunny fish wasn't as popular at the time." Today, a good quality bluefin tuna is worth thousands and will end up in some of the most exclusive restaurants. Rather than rushing to place the fish on ice and preserve its quality for eating, they would instead be hung up on the pier for locals and visitors to marvel at. Today, a statue of a bluefin tuna on a fishing line stands on the town's seafront as a nod to the association with tunny fishing. "Between the wars it did bring in a lot of money, it was a time when fishing was doing quite well here," says Vesey. "It was a thing of the moment." Indeed, the lure of big game fishing attracted famous faces of the time to the Yorkshire coast, according to Whitby Museum's natural history curator Elaine Hoyle. "It would have put both towns on the map as far as big game fishing was concerned. "Due to the existence of the Tunny Club in Scarborough, the kind of people who were going there had connections to the town through actor Charles Laughton. "His relative, Tom, was quite big in the club. These were aristocrats, politicians [and] royalty." But, as herring stocks began to decline, so too did the number of bluefin tuna. "By the 1950s there were hardly any catches and the interest was lost as well," says Vesey. The British Tunny Club is now a fish and chip shop, although memorabilia still adorns its walls. In recent years climate change has resulted in a warming of the UK's seas and major changes in marine ecosystems. According to scientists, this provides a potential explanation for the return of bluefin tuna, which have become commonplace in waters off the south west of England. Those measured in the North Sea are considerably larger and may be genetically distinct, researchers from the University of Exeter believe. They have begun tagging them to track their movements, with the data used to help manage fishing quota restrictions in the Atlantic and ensure the survival of the species. Recent catch records in the North Sea would suggest the species is in plentiful supply, with anglers confident of more given the peak season for their migration tends to run well into September. Strict fishing quotas will also help preserve stock levels here, according to Dr Lucy Hawkes, who is leading the University of Exeter research. Currently, only a small number of licence holders are allowed to fish for bluefin in order to protect their recovering numbers. "For a UK fish they are the most exciting and spectacular you can get by, no question," says Drury. "There's still a lot to learn about the species, particularly in this location. It's definitely exciting." Listen to highlights from North Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North. Microsoft has been one of the biggest tech companies for a very long time, but despite selling hardware like laptops, tablets, and (of course) Xbox consoles, it hasn't found much success in the smartphone market. Between 2010 and 2015, Microsoft released a series of smartphones running its Windows Phone operating system. However, they never gained traction, especially compared to Apple's iPhone or Google's Android. Back in 2015, BGR covered a former Microsoft engineer who discussed why the Windows Phone never really had a chance, mostly because of heavy competition and a lack of urgency on Microsoft's part. Once the iPhone launched, smartphones became Apple's top priority. At the same time, Android was becoming the second behemoth in the market and, with the help of Samsung, the only real rival to the iPhone. Apple and Android's dominance meant the deck was stacked against anyone trying to break through. If any company had the resources to succeed, it was Microsoft, but the company prioritized other projects over Windows Phone hardware and software development. Truly competing would have required Microsoft's full attention, and the company was clearly uninterested in going all-in on mobile. Setting aside the market conditions, Microsoft made some critical missteps with Windows Phone, one being Windows 8, which some critics at the time claimed had destroyed the most successful software franchise of all time. The operating system was modeled after mobile interfaces in an attempt to revitalize PCs by having them imitate the smartphone experience. However, Windows 8 had the opposite effect. Since mobile UI is based around touchscreens, it doesn't translate well to computers without them. It's why Apple has different operating systems for different categories of device rather than attempting to apply a one-size-fits-all solution. Rather than boosting its PC business, the OS was so hated by users that it damaged the entire brand for a time. Through no fault of its own, the Windows Phone became associated with Windows 8's failure. The lack of a user base also meant developers were uninterested in making apps for Windows Phone. In contrast, Google-owned Android had access to the company's many services like Gmail and YouTube, which Google pulled from Windows Phone in 2013. By 2017, even Bill Gates (then a member of the Microsoft board) and other Microsoft executives publicly admitted they had switched to Android over Windows' struggling smartphone software.  In October 2017, Microsoft ended development on Windows 10 Mobile before fully ending support in January 2020. Although the era of the Windows Phone operating system is long over, Microsoft is returning to the smartphone hardware market with the Android-powered NexPhone, expected later in 2026.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Itay Greenberg, a UK-based visual effects artist who struggled with day-trading addiction for eight years before he quit the market in 2026. Business Insider verified his trading history and debts through brokerage statements, emailed transaction records, and screenshots of his credit card portal. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I think I've always had this tendency to easily get addicted to things. It's stuff like emotional eating. One time, I placed bets on the World Cup for fun, to make the games a little bit more interesting, and after 30 minutes I lost £150. It scared me so much. I was like, "What just happened?" After my whole story with trading ended, I realized it was a warning sign. It all started with bitcoin in 2017, around Christmas. There was a friend who worked with me. He was into crypto. It sounded interesting to me. I invested around £2,000. When I talk about it now, it sounds very naive. For me, it was the fantasy of quitting my job. There's no boss. You don't need to answer to anybody. You can just do your thing and make money. Now that I can hear myself talking, I think it sounds stupid. But back then, the way it was sold to me, it kind of made sense. My wife was pregnant with our first kid. The financial stress kind of kicks in. The first year was more like, I'm going to see what happens and buy crypto coins, but it didn't really work. I didn't have the patience to just let the money sit there and do its thing. Then, my son was born. It was a very stressful time. I thought maybe I should learn how to trade. I started learning how to do it "properly." I paid for courses. I studied very hard — almost every moment I was awake. I worked with two screens: one screen was my job, and one screen was the chart. Some nights, my wife would watch TV and I would sit down and study, analyzing charts and seeing patterns. It made me think: I'm learning an occupation. I have thousands of pages of notes. It was like a university degree. That's the amount of dedication I put into it. When I lost money, in my mind I thought: I would never quit. If you lose a few trades in a row, you're thinking to yourself: Okay, it's a part of the journey — or the process, or whatever nice word you want to call it. After a certain point, I thought, I'm almost making it, and that was a very dangerous place to be. I didn't even consider losing as anything significant. I convinced myself that I'm almost there. My wife was also very convinced that I would probably make it, because she trusted me and I trusted the process. So, what's the big deal if I lose? I started jumping between different strategies and ways to trade and different platforms and different assets. At some point, I started using credit cards to hide my spending. In total, I probably spent around £30,000 to £40,000 over the years on trading (buying crypto coins, buying courses, resetting prop-trading accounts). I always say it's like death by a thousand cuts. It was always like this tiny amount, which at some point, grew bigger and bigger. The years go by, and then you realize that it's not going anywhere and you're kind of stuck in this loop. I got out of it when my son was around four or five, and we realized he probably has ADHD. I realized that there's usually a high chance that one of the parents has it. Through that, I got diagnosed. I started medication when I was 45. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. Once I got diagnosed, I kind of lost the confidence of, I can do anything. I can make it. You feel like you're under the influence of drugs or something. The real problems, you don't even deal with them. When I quit, it's like I went back to 2017, to the version of myself that was having a new baby. I never really dealt with those problems and feelings. by Jason Lemkin | Blog Posts Plus the math that has to be true for AI to reach $600B in revenue: $100K of tokens per engineer, and 30% fewer engineers. A heavy week on 20VC x SaaStr with Harry Stebbings, Rory O’Driscoll and Jason Lemkin:  Here’s what we got into: Rory’s math: At roughly 15 times current revenue, or under 10 times the $6B the company is tracking toward by year end, this is a normal multiple for the fastest-growing asset in the largest AI category. SpaceX itself trades around 40 times revenue. Buying at 15 with paper that trades at 40 is accretive the day it closes. Jason’s read: The best AI deals can often look absurdly expensive at signing and by closing, look almost conservative at closing. Don’t look at ARR multiples, look at the multiples of forward revenue and forward growth.That’s the bet. Jason’s read: We’ve been doing this show about 70-something weeks and there have probably been three different Cursors in that window. It rocketed to half a billion in revenue. Then Claude Code came out and it genuinely looked over. Nobody’s portfolio companies were using it. I’m not even sure Claude Code had launched when we started the show, which is insane to say out loud. Cursor went multimodel very early, and that one call turned into a $60B outcome. This was not linear progress. Many teams would have quit on that journey. Being agile isn’t enough at this rate of change. You have to be able to absorb a competitor shipping something better than you and keep executing your own plan anyway. Early Cursor was selling a dollar of tokens for well under a dollar. That was the standard VC mockery when we started the show. Rory’s read: The negatives you can cite along the way tend to be true. They were real. It’s easy to sound financially sophisticated and say everything eventually has to generate free cash flow, so a business without gross margins is worth nothing. That’s wrong when the market underneath is exploding, because the buyer looks past it. Coding is the biggest AI market there is, and a large share of Anthropic’s value is predicated on it. If you own the number two asset in that category and it’s compounding, margin structure is a second-order issue. The cleanest line of the episode, and the actual logic of the deal: your gross margin problem is my revenue opportunity for my Colossus cluster. Rory’s read: The set of buyers for whom this works is tiny. You need enormous compute and no obvious business sitting on top of it. That describes two companies, Meta and SpaceX. One of them bought. Cursor’s worst line item was inference paid to someone else. Owned by a buyer who owns the compute, that cost becomes internal revenue. The same P&L looks completely different depending on who holds it. Cursor was closing roughly $2B at a $50B valuation from Andreessen and others. Elon bid $60B, added a $10B breakup fee if the deal failed, and granted autonomy. That combination removed the objections. Jason’s read: Zuck did Instagram and WhatsApp in about an hour on the back of a napkin and paid high. This is the same move executed better. When a company is mid-round at a known price, you don’t run a process against it. You put a number on the table that makes the round irrelevant and you underwrite the seller’s downside if you can’t close. Very few people on earth have the authority and the currency to move that fast. Harry’s read: Meta is building model capability with Alex Wang and company and is missing the enterprise piece. Cursor would have solved that. Three reasons it went the other way: Rory’s read: owning a developer platform is existential over the medium term for exactly one company, and it isn’t AWS and it isn’t Meta. Microsoft lost its connection to developers, the group that made it in the first place. GitHub is now a trailing-edge product. That’s a serious medium-term loss even though the company is operationally fine. Also worth flagging, per Jason: the popular VC theory that one big acquisition triggers an industry-wide land grab is mostly wrong. Buyers don’t panic-buy the second or third choice because a rival moved. They buy when they realize they have less time than they thought. OpenRouter, led by Alex Atallah, is the leading LLM routing layer. Stripe’s business has always been absorbing complexity in exchange for a share of the flow. Model selection and API integration is the same shape of problem. Stripe already benefits from AI growth indirectly, taking a cut every time somebody pays OpenAI or Anthropic with a card. Rory’s read: current revenue is close to irrelevant to the price in deals like this. The acquirer is buying future extractable value, and can usually generate cash from the asset faster than the standalone company could have. In a market moving this fast, the buy-versus-build analysis that assumes a five-year build window gets abandoned. A few billion in cash and stock buys you a live capability inside a week. This is what venture returns are made of, and it happened repeatedly in the early internet buildout. Jason’s read: routing is genuinely useful for developer tools and chatbots, where availability matters more than perfectly consistent output. It’s much less useful for high-reasoning B2B workflows, where switching models introduces drift and forces constant re-testing and QA. Rippling picked a small set of models on price, performance and speed rather than managing a large menu, and that’s the more common enterprise posture. Databricks, Replit, Lovable and Vercel all do their own routing. The counterpoint: enterprises that don’t want to be captive to one frontier lab use a router as plan B, and having plan B is what keeps the lab honest on price. Rory’s read: it’s a niche product today. It could become 20% to 30% of Stripe’s revenue. It’s also entirely possible the product doesn’t exist as a product in five years, absorbed into Stripe infrastructure or reduced to a checkbox. Call it a one-in-three chance it becomes a real AI routing business, which is a fine bet at this size relative to Stripe’s market cap. OpenRouter is a TAM expansion bet. The reported interest in PayPal is a consolidation bet: use scale, strip general and administrative expense, get consumer wallets. Same acquirer, opposite logic, and both funded partly with private stock as currency. Anthropic turned its first profit on $11.5B of Q2 revenue. Gross margins went from negative in earlier years to roughly 30% last year, with an expectation of about 40% by year end. Rory’s read: when revenue moves from $4.5B a year to $10B+ in a quarter and gross margin goes from negative to 40, you can’t add expenses below the line fast enough to stop yourself from making money. Headcount and operating expense simply cannot scale that fast. Don’t expect a base case of continued profitability in an IPO filing, because compute costs keep rising, including the price increases on hardware bought from Elon. Anthropic heads toward an IPO with off-balance-sheet compute commitments and enormous stock-based comp. Rory’s read: those numbers look ugly and everyone will look through them. The only thing that matters is the growth rate in projected 2027 and 2028 revenue. The compute commitments are investments that get justified by growth, and become a millstone only if growth slows. On SBC, the distinction is real: at Workday or Salesforce, RSUs are cash comp by another name, because remove them and you have to raise salaries. At a hyper-growth company, most of that SBC number is appreciation, not recurring cost. Someone hired on a $1M package in 2023 ended up with $51M four years later. That’s not a repeatable expense line. The leniency on margins, off-balance-sheet liabilities and SBC lasts exactly as long as the growth does. The bull case has Anthropic-class revenue reaching $200B by 2028 and $600B the year after. The show did the arithmetic. The “one billion knowledge workers” framing doesn’t survive contact with global income distribution. The US is roughly 50% of the world’s high-end knowledge worker software budget and 25% of global GDP, and global software spend runs about double US spend. Inside the US there are roughly 83 million knowledge workers, but most of them are nurses and teachers, not AI replacement targets. The actual core market is the roughly 5 million people in software-adjacent roles, and they earn about $600B a year in aggregate. Rory’s read: $200B of revenue means capturing about a third of every salary dollar paid to US software workers. That’s the real bar. The variable that decides everything is the steady-state ratio of salary dollars to AI spend. Jason’s read: running 10 agents in parallel around the clock costs something close to $100,000 a year. So the model that’s emerging is $200,000 in fully loaded wages plus $100,000 of AI per person, and a team that’s 30% to 40% smaller. That’s not just developers. It’s systems administration and QA too. Run that across the US software workforce and you land at roughly $200B, call it $350B globally. Two things that make this feel real right now: a lot of companies have started capping AI budgets after spend went exponential over the last 60 days, and CFOs are starting to use the $100K per head number as the justification for holding engineering headcount flat. The dispersion is enormous. Ramp data has the top 1% of tech-forward spenders at about $7,000 per month while the median sits near $100. At the top end, AI spend reaches 50 cents for every dollar of salary. Jason’s read: the fastest companies are already working on their 2027 roadmaps. That’s the tell that AI spend has crossed from performative into productive. If you’re still running quarterly and monthly planning cycles in an agentic environment and you haven’t finished this year’s product goals, you’re behind, and the gap compounds. Rory’s caution: the surveys show wide dispersion, with many companies spending far less per head than the leaders. The bet is that spend correlates with output. That correlation is a hypothesis, not a proven fact, and it’s the single most important open question in the $200B math. Jason’s read: Anthropic can go public with a profitable quarter and an enterprise leadership position. That’s a good first impression, and going later is a risk if either the company’s growth or the public market decelerates. Rory’s read: OpenAI has a harder path after executive turmoil and a slower first half, and probably prices more precisely and less enthusiastically as the second one out. Long run the ordering doesn’t matter much. Short run it does, because both companies have enormous ongoing capital needs, and even pre-IPO OpenAI can sell stock at a discount to its implicit valuation. Price clears every market. The terms are what’s uncertain. Related, and a good signal on how AI companies now think about GTM: Denise Dresser is out as OpenAI’s CRO and Dali Rajic is in. AI companies are hiring Salesforce operators to scale the way the last generation hired out of Oracle, but the preference at the top is for leaders forged in hyper-competitive environments like Wiz rather than classic B2B motions like Slack. Workday stock jumped 18% on the news. The structure is a large equity check plus substantial debt, using roughly $3B of annual cash flow on $10B of revenue at about 35% operating margins to service it, aiming at a 20% IRR over five years. Rory’s read: this is a mature-phase transaction, not a growth one. Unlike venture, where entry price barely matters if you’re right, this is precise financial engineering. Overpay by 20% to 30% and your IRR falls to the low teens. The base case for a system of record growing 13% is about 5.3 times revenue. Software that isn’t a system of record, or that grows slower, prices closer to 2.7 times. Set that against OpenRouter changing hands near 70 times trailing revenue and you have the entire market in two numbers. Aneel Bhusri already came back after hiring a successor, which tells you the board thinks AI changed the job. If Silver Lake runs an agentic transformation with the founder leading it, the upside case is real. Rory’s read: Workday is closed, which buffers it from agents siphoning value. Salesforce is open, which is why Gong, Outreach and Salesloft exist on top of it and why nothing equivalent exists on Workday. Open ecosystems get more innovation and give more of the value away. In the end, the money in an ecosystem gravitates toward the general ledger. Jason’s read: running Salesforce headless, with agents doing the interacting, makes the software far more useful and simultaneously far easier to abstract away. High logo retention is not the same as safety. The environment is grow or die, and holding customers hostage inside a system of record does not produce growth. CIOs are actively trying to pay 80% or 90% of last year’s bill even on contracts they’re locked into. Where this bites: private equity buying at 10 to 12 times revenue with no growth plan ends in a death spiral against the debt and a mid-teens IRR. Bending Spoons can triple prices, lose 20% of customers and come out ahead. That’s a strategy, not a business. Companies with no AI in the product and a thick middle management layer are the most exposed group in software right now. Higgsfield raised at $5.5B on roughly $700M ARR. Lovable raised from Menlo at $13.3B on something in the $600M to $700M range. Same revenue, more than double the price. Jason’s read: Lovable and Replit were mediocre products when this show started and are now generationally good. Both added automatic deep security penetration testing. Cursor is expanding into things like Origin and could plausibly replace the GitHub workflow. Adjusted for platform complexity, Lovable’s price is comparable to what Cursor commanded. Coding is also simply a deeper market than enterprise video, which is real but smaller. What both did right: start with high-volume consumer demand, website building and coding for one, video for the other, then layer mid-market and enterprise on top. Classic PLG, executed in an AI cycle. Rory’s read on moats: in new software markets, moats start light and accrete with execution. Netscape and MS-DOS both started simple. Every feature you add makes a viable alternative harder to build. Model development and bioinformatics are genuinely IP-dependent. Most software is not, and wins on being faster and better. These companies are also now talent magnets, and that becomes its own barrier. One company raised $700M at $21B from Jane Street, Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia and Andreessen, three weeks after closing at $10B. Jason’s read: you can now raise on one good month. Two years ago you needed three or four. The related story: the DOJ is looking at Andreessen over overlapping board seats, triggered during the Fivetran and dbt merger review and extending to Databricks and Fivetran. Section 8 of the Clayton Act, which dates to the early 1900s, bars a person from sitting on two competing boards. Whether two different partners from the same firm counts is much less clear. Precedent, including Thoma Bravo’s, is that the firm removes a director and everyone moves on. Low drama, low consequence. Four transactions, one behavior. SpaceX paid $10B over an existing round to compress a build into a week. Stripe paid roughly 70 times trailing revenue for routing infrastructure it could have built. Silver Lake is paying 5.3 times for predictability instead. And Anthropic is spending against compute commitments that only make sense if 2027 revenue arrives on schedule. For founders, the practical version is narrower. The buyers who pay these prices are the ones for whom your worst cost line is their existing asset. If that buyer doesn’t exist for your category, the gross margin criticism you’re brushing off is going to be the thing that decides your outcome. Cursor had that buyer. Upon its completion in 2026, the SunZia Wind Farm became the largest project of its kind in the Western Hemisphere, capable of 3.5-gigawatts. Located in New Mexico, SunZia marks a huge milestone for the United States in the world of renewable energy with a peak capacity that can power roughly one million homes per year. The majority of the turbines — 674 out of 916, to be exact — were supplied by GE Vernova. Based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, GE Vernova is a top manufacturer of wind turbines in the U.S. representing 56% of this market as of 2024, and, in 2025, GE Vernova along with Danish rival, Vestas, accounted for 93% of America's onshore wind turbines installations. Moreover, GE Vernova alone is responsible for about 59,000 wind turbine installations globally, including 35,000 in the U.S., allowing the company to boast that its technology helps generate almost a quarter of the world's electricity. GE Vernova may be the biggest names in this field, but there are a handful of other turbine manufacturers contributing to the global renewable energy supply, and they're all making waves. While GE Vernova might dominate the U.S. supply, rivals such as Vestas, Siemens Gamesa, and Goldwind are all hitting international milestones. In 2025, Vestas was the first manufacturer to pass the 200-gigawatt cumulatively supplied threshold, not GE Vernova. In fact, two of the five companies have a higher cumulative supply alongside Vestas, including Goldwind with 163 gigawatts and Siemens Gamesa with 148 gigawatts. GE Vernova came in fourth with 125 gigawatts. In addition, these names represent four of the five companies that have passed the milestone of over 100-gigawatts of renewable wind power installed, which is "enough electricity to power many of the world's largest economies." Globally, renewable wind energy satisfies about 9.5% of electricity demand, with a record 178-gigawatts of wind power coming online in 2025, a 40% increase over years prior. Upwards trend or not, none of these companies have anything on China's new flying wind turbine, which is designed to float in the air, like a balloon, and help unlock power that conventional options could never reach. With global energy demand growing for several reasons, and nuclear energy serving as a viable alternative to conventional power, it begs the question how many wind turbines equal a single nuclear reactor? The short answer is that it would take a farm with about 800 turbines – with each turbine producing about 3 megawatts – to equal a single nuclear reactor.  It does take a lot more wind turbines and a lot more space to match the capacity of nuclear power, but turbines are more recyclable when they reach end of their life. Wind turbines last about 20 to 30 years, compared to nuclear reactors, which have a tentative lifespan about 40 years, but to date, about 94% of a wind turbine's parts can be recycled, including the foundation, tower, gear box, generator, and even more recently, the rotor blades. When you compare wind versus solar, though, wind energy is technically more efficient and more readily available, believe it or not. Even a light breeze can generate energy with a proper wind turbine installation.

There are hundreds of 12V-port charging adapters on the market, but if you've noticed that your 12V port is doing a bad job at charging your mobile tech, the issue may have more to do with the adapter you're using than the port itself. While Epic has spent much of this year promising a launcher overhaul, including a faster, redesigned storefront with tailored recommendations and quicker ways to browse, one industry analyst has revealed that it might not be enough. Speaking to PC Gamer, Emmanuel Rosier, director of market intelligence at Newzoo, admitted, "I don't see how they can recover at this point". Rosier's argument centres on Steam's unshakeable grip on the market, with Epic's free game giveaways doing little to build lasting engagement, pointing out that a giveaway can sometimes end up boosting a game's sales on Steam instead, as players stick to one launcher rather than fragment their collection. "I don't really see how they can turn that around because Steam has become so inevitable," he said. "The Epic Games Store, they get players by giving free games, but people just go, they log in, they get the free games, they don't even play them. You know, it's almost like collecting games rather than actually playing them. "The challenge I think Epic is facing is that they try to win everywhere in the past few years," Rosier added. "They try to win against Steam, they try to win against Apple, against Google Play, and probably they run out of steam on where they cannot fight all these battles at the same time." Rosier was considerably more upbeat about Epic's prospects as a developer than as a storefront operator, however, pointing to renewed focus on Fortnite as a rare bright spot. He highlighted the growing use of crossover cosmetics from other publishers' games, pointing to Sonic the Hedgehog and Pac-Man rubbing shoulders with Kingdom Hearts' Sora and Persona 5's Joker in Fortnite's current season. "You can see they put a lot of thought in Fortnite right now," he said. "They are doing everything they can, and I think it's working better when you look at the state of Fortnite today compared to six months or one year ago." Ultimately, though, Rosier's assessment of the Epic Games Store itself was less enthusiastic, suggesting it is increasingly unlikely to ever seriously challenge Steam as a storefront.
